chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from 'Asim ibn Humayd from Muhammad ibn Qays from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) ruled regarding a slave who calls a free man his father (other than his actual father): He said, 'I see that his skin should be stripped (exposed for flogging).'
And he said regarding a man who was called (by another) to be his father: 'Present your proof, and I will enable you against him.'
So when he brought the proof, he said, 'Indeed, his mother was a slave-girl.'
He said, 'There is no full hadd punishment upon you for his cursing, just as he cursed you, or pardon him.'
What this report contains from his saying 'I see that his skin should be exposed' implies that he may have meant that his skin should be exposed so that the hadd punishment is carried out upon him.

And it implies that the meaning is if his mother was a slave-girl and he attributed her to zina (fornication), then the full hadd is not obligatory upon him, but ta'zir (discretionary punishment) is obligatory upon him.

And there is in the hadith something that weakens reliance upon it, which is that Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said to him, 'Curse him as he cursed you.' And it is not permissible for him (peace be upon him) to order cursing, because cursing is ugly (improper), and he only has the right to carry out the hadd upon him, either the full one or ta'zir.

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (Ali ibn Abi Talib)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling for a slave who falsely claims a free man is his father?
ai.summary: This narration from *Al-Istibsar* details Imam Ali’s juridical reasoning in *qadhf* (false accusation of adultery) cases involving slaves, specifically distinguishing between the fixed *hadd* penalty and discretionary *ta'zir* based on the mother’s status. The text highlights a scholarly nuance: while Ali suggested 'expose his skin,' this may refer to the physical act of flogging for punishment rather than the verbal act of cursing, resolving the apparent contradiction in the phrase 'curse him as he cursed you.' This reflects the Shia emphasis on precise legal interpretation (*ijtihad*) within the broader framework of justice and proportionality in penal law.
